accuracy.evidence: Checked against Common Core L.5.2d (use underlining, quotation marks, or italics to indicate titles of works) and the whole-versus-part convention in the Chicago Manual of Style, chapter 8 (italics for books, periodicals, films, albums, TV series; quotation marks for articles, chapters, poems, songs, episodes) and the Purdue OWL titles guide. Underlining as the handwritten stand-in for italics matches Purdue OWL. Title-case rules (first, last and major words capitalised; articles, short conjunctions and prepositions lower case mid-title) follow Chicago's title-case rules in chapter 8. Example facts checked: The Reader of Books is chapter 1 of Matilda, Ordinary is the first chapter of Wonder, the Wonder film was released in 2017, Let It Go is a song from Frozen, Thriller is a 1982 album. Lab sentences avoid a full stop or comma straight after a closing quotation mark, so no US/UK placement rule is taught by accident.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the real slips: choosing italics because a work is famous or long (the Let It Go prediction, the m3 item, the sort step's done line 'Fame does not decide: whole or part does'), quotation marks on book titles (sort, medium and fix feedback), writing a whole work by hand in quotation marks instead of underlining (Paddington prediction and challenge), underlining typed text, capitalising every word including in and the (The Cat In The Hat distractor), treating a short verb as a little word (Where the Wild Things Are prediction), and dropping the style on a second mention (review step, m6, challenge).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagtitle renders titles in real italics, underline and curly quotation marks on the canvas through its own rich-text layout, which no other flagship has. Its steps are about this topic only: a two-bin whole/part sorter, a typed-versus-handwritten style chooser, a tap-to-capitalise title strip that refuses little words with a reason, a drag-a-style token onto each title in a sentence, and a slip finder over a five-line book review. flagcomma, flagdspeech and flagnamecap teach other punctuation. lab_distinct stayed under 30% against every flagship lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner discovers the rule by sorting: each placement explains itself ('Let It Go is one song from the film: a part, so “Let It Go”'), a wrong drop names what the title is part of, and the finished bins show every whole title in italics beside every part in quotation marks. In the capitals step, tapping the gives 'The is a little word in the middle of the title, so it stays small', while tapping Are capitalises it with 'it is the last word, and a verb'. Finished sentences stay rendered with their styles at the end of each step.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions hold a tempting wrong answer the lab then disproves: 'Italics: it is famous' for Let It Go (the sorter only accepts the part box), 'Put Paddington in quotation marks' for handwriting (the chooser rejects quotation marks for a film and explains underlining), and 'No: it is a short word' for are in Where the Wild Things Are (the strip capitalises Are).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating challenge questions with twelve wrong-answer messages that each name the slip: quotation marks for a whole book, capitals without italics, italics or underlining for a single song, quotation marks or plain text for a handwritten film, every-word capitals versus missing capitals on main words, styling the newspaper instead of the article, and switching or dropping the style on a second mention.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs use short sentences and concrete examples (A song is one part of an album.) at FK grade 1.8 against the family kid target of 5.0. The adult text uses the precise terms italics, quotation marks, underlining, title case, whole work and house style at FK grade 6.6 against the 10.0 target.

no_filler.evidence: The content gate found no banned phrases, and the explanation stayed under 12% six-word overlap with every other lesson, including Capitals for Names, Days and I and Punctuating Direct Speech. Every lab message names the title and what kind of work it is.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at 360 px (touch, 1.5x) in light and dark for every step before and after Show me: the two sort bins list all eight finished titles without overlap, the three style tiles show italics, underline and quotation marks at full width, title-word chips wrap onto two rows, the two title targets and two style tokens sit side by side, and all five review lines fit. The medium sentence was moved up after the first dark screenshot showed a wrapped line touching its subtitle.

accessibility.evidence: The browser gate completed every task with Show me on desktop and iPhone 13, the challenge showed, and axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) found no violations in light or dark. Every canvas action has a labelled button ('Charlotte's Web is a whole work', 'Show the title with underline', 'Give witch a capital', 'Put Moana in italics', 'Slip in: My friend thinks Wonder is too sad.'), and the canvas aria-label is rewritten with every message. A fuzz pass clicking every button in every step produced no console errors.

sources: Common Core State Standards for English Language Arts, Language L.5.2d
The Chicago Manual of Style, 17th edition, chapter 8: titles of works and title case
Purdue Online Writing Lab: Using italics and underlining; Quotation marks with titles
National Curriculum in England: English Appendix 2 (capital letters for proper nouns)
